# modular_bitfield - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/modular-bitfield/

## Expand description

Provides macros to support bitfield structs allowing for modular use of bit-enums.

The mainly provided macros are [ #[bitfield]](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html) for structs and

[for enums that shall be usable within bitfield structs.](https://docs.rs/trait.Specifier.html)

`#[derive(Specifier)]`There are preset bitfield specifiers such as `B1`, `B2`,..,`B64`
that allow for easy bitfield usage in structs very similar to how
they work in C or C++.

- Performance of the macro generated code is as fast as its hand-written alternative.
- Compile-time checks allow for safe usage of bitfield structs and enums.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Annotate a Rust struct with the [ #[bitfield]](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html) attribute in order to convert it into a bitfield,
with

[optional parameters](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html#parameters)that control how the bitfield is generated. The

`B1`, `B2`, … `B128` prelude types can be used as primitives to declare the number of bits per field.```
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: B1,
    status: B2,
}
```
This produces a `new` constructor as well as a variety of getters and setters that
allows to interact with the bitfield in a safe fashion:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-constructors)Example: Constructors

```
let data = PackedData::new()
    .with_header(1)
    .with_body(2)
    .with_is_alive(0)
    .with_status(3);
assert_eq!(data.header(), 1);
assert_eq!(data.body(), 2);
assert_eq!(data.is_alive(), 0);
assert_eq!(data.status(), 3);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-primitive-types)Example: Primitive Types

Any type that implements the `Specifier` trait can be used as a bitfield field.
Besides the already mentioned `B1`, .. `B128` also the `bool`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`,
`u64` or `u128` primitive types can be used from prelude.

We can use this knowledge to encode our `is_alive` as `bool` type instead of `B1`:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: B2,
}
let mut data = PackedData::new()
    .with_is_alive(true);
assert!(data.is_alive());
data.set_is_alive(false);
assert!(!data.is_alive());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-enum-specifiers)Example: Enum Specifiers

It is possible to derive the `Specifier` trait for `enum` types very easily to make
them also usable as a field within a bitfield type:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow, None,
}
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: Status,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-extra-safety-guard)Example: Extra Safety Guard

In order to make sure that our `Status` enum still requires exatly 2 bit we can add
`#[bits = 2]` to its field:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    status: Status,
}
```
Setting and getting our new `status` field is naturally as follows:

```
let mut data = PackedData::new()
    .with_status(Status::Green);
assert_eq!(data.status(), Status::Green);
data.set_status(Status::Red);
assert_eq!(data.status(), Status::Red);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-skipping-fields)Example: Skipping Fields

It might make sense to only allow users to set or get information from a field or
even to entirely disallow interaction with a bitfield. For this the `#[skip]` attribute
can be used on a bitfield of a `#[bitfield]` annotated struct.

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct SomeBitsUndefined {
    #[skip(setters)]
    read_only: bool,
    #[skip(getters)]
    write_only: bool,
    #[skip]
    unused: B6,
}
```
It is possible to use `#[skip(getters, setters)]` or `#[skip(getters)]` followed by a `#[skip(setters)]`
attribute applied on the same bitfield. The effects are the same. When skipping both, getters and setters,
it is possible to completely avoid having to specify a name:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct SomeBitsUndefined {
    #[skip] __: B2,
    is_activ: bool,
    #[skip] __: B2,
    is_received: bool,
    #[skip] __: B2,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-unfilled-bitfields)Example: Unfilled Bitfields

Sometimes it might be useful to not be required to construct a bitfield that defines
all bits and therefore is required to have a bit width divisible by 8. In this case
you can use the `filled: bool` parameter of the `#[bitfield]` macro in order to toggle
this for your respective bitfield:

```
#[bitfield(filled = false)]
pub struct SomeBitsUndefined {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    pre_status: B3,
}
```
In the above example `SomeBitsUndefined` only defines the first 5 bits and leaves the rest
3 bits of its entire 8 bits undefined. The consequences are that its generated `from_bytes`
method is fallible since it must guard against those undefined bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-recursive-bitfields)Example: Recursive Bitfields

It is possible to use `#[bitfield]` structs as fields of `#[bitfield]` structs.
This is generally useful if there are some common fields for multiple bitfields
and is achieved by adding the `#[derive(Specifier)]` attribute to the struct
annotated with `#[bitfield]`:

```
#[bitfield(filled = false)]
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub struct Header {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    pre_status: Status,
}
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: Header,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: Status,
}
```
With the `bits: int` parameter of the `#[bitfield]` macro on the `Header` struct and the
`#[bits: int]` attribute of the `#[derive(Specifier)]` on the `Status` enum we
can have additional compile-time guarantees about the bit widths of the resulting entities:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
#[bits = 2]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow, None,
}
#[bitfield(bits = 4)]
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub struct Header {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    pre_status: Status,
}
#[bitfield(bits = 16)]
pub struct PackedData {
    #[bits = 4]
    header: Header,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    status: Status,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-advanced-enum-specifiers)Example: Advanced Enum Specifiers

For our `Status` enum we actually just need 3 status variants: `Green`, `Yellow` and `Red`.
We introduced the `None` status variants because `Specifier` enums by default are required
to have a number of variants that is a power of two. We can ship around this by specifying
`#[bits = 2]` on the top and get rid of our placeholder `None` variant while maintaining
the invariant of it requiring 2 bits:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
#[bits = 2]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow,
}
```
However, having such enums now yields the possibility that a bitfield might contain invalid bit
patterns for such fields. We can safely access those fields with protected getters. For the sake
of demonstration we will use the generated `from_bytes` constructor with which we can easily
construct bitfields that may contain invalid bit patterns:

```
let mut data = PackedData::from_bytes([0b0000_0000, 0b1100_0000]);
//           The 2 status field bits are invalid -----^^
//           as Red = 0x00, Green = 0x01 and Yellow = 0x10
assert_eq!(data.status_or_err(), Err(InvalidBitPattern::new(0b11)));
data.set_status(Status::Green);
assert_eq!(data.status_or_err(), Ok(Status::Green));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#generated-implementations)Generated Implementations

For the example `#[bitfield]` struct the following implementations are going to be generated:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct Example {
    a: bool,
    b: B7,
}
```
| Signature | Description |
|---|---|
| `fn new() -> Self` | Creates a new instance of the bitfield with all bits initialized to 0. |
| `fn from_bytes([u8; 1]) -> Self` | Creates a new instance of the bitfield from the given raw bytes. |
| `fn into_bytes(self) -> [u8; 1]` | Returns the underlying bytes of the bitfield. |

And below the generated signatures for field `a`:

| Signature | Description |
|---|---|
| `fn a() -> bool` | Returns the value of `a`or panics if invalid. |
| `fn a_or_err() -> Result<bool, InvalidBitPattern<u8>>` | Returns the value of `a`of an error providing information about the invalid bits. |
| `fn set_a(&mut self, new_value: bool)` | Sets `a`to the new value or panics if`new_value`contains invalid bits. |
| `fn set_a_checked(&mut self, new_value: bool) -> Result<(), OutOfBounds>` | Sets `a`to the new value of returns an out of bounds error. |
| `fn with_a(self, new_value: bool) -> Self` | Similar to `set_a`but useful for method chaining. |
| `fn with_a_checked(self, new_value: bool) -> Result<Self, OutOfBounds>` | Similar to `set_a_checked`but useful for method chaining. |

Getters for unnamed fields in tuple-like structs are prefixed with `get_`
(e.g. `get_0()`, `get_1_or_err()`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#generated-structure)Generated Structure

From David Tolnay’s procedural macro workshop:

The macro conceptualizes given structs as a sequence of bits 0..N. The bits are grouped into fields in the order specified by the struct written by the user.

The `#[bitfield]` attribute rewrites the caller’s struct into a private byte array representation
with public getter and setter methods for each field.
The total number of bits N is required to be a multiple of 8: This is checked at compile time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following invocation builds a struct with a total size of 32 bits or 4 bytes.
It places field `a` in the least significant bit of the first byte,
field `b` in the next three least significant bits,
field `c` in the remaining four most significant bits of the first byte,
and field `d` spanning the next three bytes.

```
use modular_bitfield::prelude::*;
#[bitfield]
pub struct MyFourBytes {
    a: B1,
    b: B3,
    c: B4,
    d: B24,
}
```
```
                               least significant bit of third byte
                                 ┊           most significant
                                 ┊             ┊
                                 ┊             ┊
║  first byte   ║  second byte  ║  third byte   ║  fourth byte  ║
╟───────────────╫───────────────╫───────────────╫───────────────╢
║▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒║
╟─╫─────╫───────╫───────────────────────────────────────────────╢
║a║  b  ║   c   ║                       d                       ║
                 ┊                                             ┊
                 ┊                                             ┊
               least significant bit of d         most significant
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Errors that can occur while operating on modular bitfields.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- The prelude: `use modular_bitfield::prelude::*;`
- [specifiers](https://docs.rs/specifiers/index.html)
- The default set of predefined specifiers.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Specifier](https://docs.rs/trait.Specifier.html)
- The `Specifier`trait describes a sequence of bits stored in an integer primitive (the`Bytes``InOut`

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [bitfield](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html)
- Applicable to structs to turn their fields into compact bitfields.

# modular_bitfield - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/modular-bitfield/0.13.1/modular_bitfield/

## Expand description

Provides macros to support bitfield structs allowing for modular use of bit-enums.

The mainly provided macros are [ #[bitfield]](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html) for structs and

[for enums that shall be usable within bitfield structs.](https://docs.rs/trait.Specifier.html)

`#[derive(Specifier)]`There are preset bitfield specifiers such as `B1`, `B2`,..,`B64`
that allow for easy bitfield usage in structs very similar to how
they work in C or C++.

- Performance of the macro generated code is as fast as its hand-written alternative.
- Compile-time checks allow for safe usage of bitfield structs and enums.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Annotate a Rust struct with the [ #[bitfield]](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html) attribute in order to convert it into a bitfield,
with

[optional parameters](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html#parameters)that control how the bitfield is generated. The

`B1`, `B2`, … `B128` prelude types can be used as primitives to declare the number of bits per field.```

pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: B1,
    status: B2,
}
```
This produces a `new` constructor as well as a variety of getters and setters that
allows to interact with the bitfield in a safe fashion:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-constructors)Example: Constructors

```

    .with_header(1)
    .with_body(2)
    .with_is_alive(0)
    .with_status(3);

assert_eq!(data.body(), 2);
assert_eq!(data.is_alive(), 0);
assert_eq!(data.status(), 3);
```

    .with_is_alive(true);

data.set_is_alive(false);

[§](https://docs.rs#example-skipping-fields)Example: Skipping Fields

It might make sense to only allow users to set or get information from a field or

```

```

[§](https://docs.rs#example-recursive-bitfields)Example: Recursive Bitfields

It is possible to use `#[bitfield]` structs as fields of `#[bitfield]` structs.
This is generally useful if there are some common fields for multiple bitfields
and is achieved by adding the `#[derive(Specifier)]` attribute to the struct
annotated with `#[bitfield]`:

```
#[bitfield(filled = false)]
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub struct Header {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    pre_status: Status,
}
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: Header,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: Status,
}
```
With the `bits: int` parameter of the `#[bitfield]` macro on the `Header` struct and the
`#[bits: int]` attribute of the `#[derive(Specifier)]` on the `Status` enum we
can have additional compile-time guarantees about the bit widths of the resulting entities:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
#[bits = 2]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow, None,
}
#[bitfield(bits = 4)]
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub struct Header {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    pre_status: Status,
}
#[bitfield(bits = 16)]
pub struct PackedData {
    #[bits = 4]
    header: Header,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    status: Status,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-advanced-enum-specifiers)Example: Advanced Enum Specifiers

For our `Status` enum we actually just need 3 status variants: `Green`, `Yellow` and `Red`.
We introduced the `None` status variants because `Specifier` enums by default are required
to have a number of variants that is a power of two. We can ship around this by specifying
`#[bits = 2]` on the top and get rid of our placeholder `None` variant while maintaining
the invariant of it requiring 2 bits:

```

    Red, Green, Yellow,
}
```
However, having such enums now yields the possibility that a bitfield might contain invalid bit
patterns for such fields. We can safely access those fields with protected getters. For the sake
of demonstration we will use the generated `from_bytes` constructor with which we can easily
construct bitfields that may contain invalid bit patterns:

```

//           The 2 status field bits are invalid -----^^
//           as Red = 0x00, Green = 0x01 and Yellow = 0x10
assert_eq!(data.status_or_err(), Err(InvalidBitPattern::new(0b11)));
data.set_status(Status::Green);
assert_eq!(data.status_or_err(), Ok(Status::Green));
```

For the example `#[bitfield]` struct the following implementations are going to be generated:

    a: bool,
    b: B7,
}

| Signature | Description |
|---|---|
| `fn new() -> Self` | Creates a new instance of the bitfield with all bits initialized to 0. |
| `fn from_bytes([u8; 1]) -> Self` | Creates a new instance of the bitfield from the given raw bytes. |

(e.g. `get_0()`, `get_1_or_err()`, etc.).

# modular-bitfield 0.13.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/modular-bitfield/latest

# Modular Bitfields for Rust

- `no_std`: Supports embedded development without- `std`library.
- This crate uses and generates 100% safe Rust code.

## Description

Allows to have bitfield structs and enums as bitfield specifiers that work very similar to C and C++ bitfields.

## Advantages

- **Safety:**Macro embraced enums and structs are checked for valid structure during compilation time.
- **Speed:**Generated code is as fast as handwritten code. (See benchmarks below.)
- **Modularity:**Enums can be used modular within bitfield structs.

## Attribution

Implements the `#[bitfield]` macros introduced and specified in David Tolnay's [procedural macro workshop](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop/blob/master/README.md).

Thanks go to David Tolnay for designing the specification for the macros implemented in this crate.

## Usage

Annotate a Rust struct with the `#[bitfield]` attribute in order to convert it into a bitfield.
The `B1`, `B2`, ... `B128` prelude types can be used as primitives to declare the number of bits per field.

```
```
This produces a `new` constructor as well as a variety of getters and setters that
allows to interact with the bitfield in a safe fashion:

### Example: Constructors

```
let data = new
    .with_header
    .with_body
    .with_is_alive
    .with_status;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
### Example: Primitive Types

Any type that implements the `Specifier` trait can be used as a bitfield field.
Besides the already mentioned `B1`, .. `B128` also the `bool`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`,
`u64` or `u128` primitive types can be used from prelude.

We can use this knowledge to encode our `is_alive` as `bool` type instead of `B1`:

```
let mut data = new
    .with_is_alive;
assert!;
data.set_is_alive;
assert!;
```
### Example: Enum Specifiers

It is possible to derive the `Specifier` trait for `enum` types very easily to make
them also usable as a field within a bitfield type:

```
```
### Example: Extra Safety Guard

In order to make sure that our `Status` enum still requires exatly 2 bit we can add
`#[bits = 2]` to its field:

```
```
Setting and getting our new `status` field is naturally as follows:

```
let mut data = new
    .with_status;
assert_eq!;
data.set_status;
assert_eq!;
```
### Example: Recursive Bitfields

It is possible to use `#[bitfield]` structs as fields of `#[bitfield]` structs.
This is generally useful if there are some common fields for multiple bitfields
and is achieved by adding `#[derive(Specifier)]` to the attributes of the
`#[bitfield]` annotated struct:

```
```
With the `bits: int` parameter of the `#[bitfield]` macro on the `Header` struct and the
`#[bits: int]` attribute of the `#[derive(Specifier)]` on the `Status` enum we
can have additional compile-time guarantees about the bit widths of the resulting entities:

```
```
### Example: Advanced Enum Specifiers

For our `Status` enum we actually just need 3 status variants: `Green`, `Yellow` and `Red`.
We introduced the `None` status variants because `Specifier` enums by default are required
to have a number of variants that is a power of two. We can ship around this by specifying
`#[bits = 2]` on the top and get rid of our placeholder `None` variant while maintaining
the invariant of it requiring 2 bits:

```
# use *;
```
However, having such enums now yields the possibility that a bitfield might contain invalid bit
patterns for such fields. We can safely access those fields with protected getters. For the sake
of demonstration we will use the generated `from_bytes` constructor with which we can easily
construct bitfields that may contain invalid bit patterns:

```
let mut data = from_bytes;
//           The 2 status field bits are invalid -----^^
//           as Red = 0x00, Green = 0x01 and Yellow = 0x10
assert_eq!;
data.set_status;
assert_eq!;
```
## Benchmarks

Below are some benchmarks between the [hand-written code](https://github.com/modular-bitfield/modular-bitfield/blob/master/benches/handwritten.rs) and the macro-generated code for some example getters and setters that cover a decent variety of use cases.

We can conclude that the macro-generated code is as fast as hand-written code would be. Please file a PR if you see a way to improve either side.

- `cargo bench`to run the benchmarks
- `cargo test --benches`to run the benchmark tests

### Summary

The `modular_bitfield` crate generates bitfields that are ...

- just as efficient as the handwritten alternatives.
- equally efficient or more efficient than the alternative [bitfield](https://crates.io/crates/bitfield)crate.

# static_assertions - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/static_assertions/^1.1/

## Expand description

Assertions to ensure correct assumptions about constants, types, and more.

*All* checks provided by this crate are performed at [compile-time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compile_time). This
allows for finding errors quickly and early when it comes to ensuring
certain features or aspects of a codebase. These macros are especially
important when exposing a public API that requires types to be the same size
or implement certain traits.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

This crate is available [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/static_assertions) and can be used by adding the
following to your project’s [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html):

```
[dependencies]
static_assertions = "1.1.0"
```
and this to your crate root (`main.rs` or `lib.rs`):

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate static_assertions;
```
When using [Rust 2018 edition](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2018/12/06/Rust-1.31-and-rust-2018.html#rust-2018), the following shorthand can help if
having `#[macro_use]` is undesirable.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Very thorough examples are provided in the docs for
[each individual macro](https://docs.rs#macros). Failure case examples are also documented.

[§](https://docs.rs#changes)Changes

See [ CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/nvzqz/static-assertions-rs/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md)
for an exhaustive list of what has changed from one version to another.

[§](https://docs.rs#donate)Donate

This project is made freely available (as in free beer), but unfortunately
not all beer is free! So, if you would like to buy me a beer (or coffee or
*more*), then consider supporting my work that’s benefited your project
and thousands of others.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_cfg.html)- cfg
- Asserts that a given configuration is set.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_align.html)- eq_ - align
- Asserts that types are equal in alignment.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_size.html)- eq_ - size
- Asserts that types are equal in size.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_size_ptr.html)- eq_ - size_ - ptr
- Asserts that values pointed to are equal in size.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq_size_val.html)- eq_ - size_ - val
- Asserts that values are equal in size.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_fields.html)- fields
- Asserts that the type has the given fields.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_all.html)- impl_ - all
- Asserts that the type implements *all*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_any.html)- impl_ - any
- Asserts that the type implements *any*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_impl_one.html)- impl_ - one
- Asserts that the type implements exactly one in a set of traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_not_impl_all.html)- not_ - impl_ - all
- Asserts that the type does **not**implement*all*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_not_impl_any.html)- not_ - impl_ - any
- Asserts that the type does **not**implement*any*of the given traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_obj_safe.html)- obj_ - safe
- Asserts that the traits support dynamic dispatch
([object-safety](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch17-02-trait-objects.html#object-safety-is-required-for-trait-objects)).
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_trait_sub_all.html)- trait_ - sub_ - all
- Asserts that the trait is a child of all of the other traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_trait_super_all.html)- trait_ - super_ - all
- Asserts that the trait is a parent of all of the other traits.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_type_eq_all.html)- type_ - eq_ - all
- Asserts that *all*types in a list are equal to each other.
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_type_ne_all.html)- type_ - ne_ - all
- Asserts that *all*types are**not**equal to each other.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/macro.const_assert.html)- assert
- Asserts that constant expressions evaluate to `true`.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/macro.const_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Asserts that constants are equal in value.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/macro.const_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Asserts that constants are **not**equal in value.

# bitfield - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bitfield/^0.19/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros to generate bitfield-like struct.

See the documentation of the macros for how to use them.

Examples and tests are also a great way to understand how to use these macros.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bitfield](https://docs.rs/macro.bitfield.html)
- Combines `bitfield_bitrange`and`bitfield_fields`.
- [bitfield_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitfield_bitrange.html)- bitrange
- Implements `BitRange`and`BitRangeMut`for a tuple struct (or “newtype”).
- [bitfield_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitfield_constructor.html)- constructor
- Implements an exhaustive constructor function for a bitfield. Should only be called by `bitfield!`when using`impl new;`
- [bitfield_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitfield_debug.html)- debug
- Generates a `fmt::Debug`implementation.
- [bitfield_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitfield_fields.html)- fields
- Declares the fields of a struct.
- [bitfield_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitfield_impl.html)- impl
- Generates and dispatches trait implementations for a struct
- [check_](https://docs.rs/macro.check_msb_lsb_order.html)- msb_ - lsb_ - order
- Internal use macro, that `debug_assert`than msb >= lsb and thus they are not inverted

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Bit](https://docs.rs/trait.Bit.html)
- A trait to get a single bit.
- [BitMut](https://docs.rs/trait.BitMut.html)
- A trait to set a single bit.
- [BitRange](https://docs.rs/trait.BitRange.html)
- A trait to get ranges of bits.
- [BitRange](https://docs.rs/trait.BitRangeMut.html)- Mut
- A trait to set ranges of bits.

# tiny_bench - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tiny-bench/^0.4/

## Expand description

`tiny-bench`, a tiny benchmarking library.
The crate is divided into two sections, benchmarking and timing.
Benchmarking provides tools to measure code execution, show statistics about that execution,
and compare those statistics to previous runs.
Timing provides tools to time code. Timing how long a closure runs, or how long an iterator runs.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkConfig.html)- Config
- Struct containing all of the configuration options for a benchmark.
- [Timed](https://docs.rs/struct.TimedIterator.html)- Iterator
- An iterator that wraps another iterator and times each call to `next`
- [Timing](https://docs.rs/struct.TimingData.html)- Data
- Data collected after a timed run

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Timeable](https://docs.rs/trait.Timeable.html)
- A trait for allowing iterators to be used as timers

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bench](https://docs.rs/fn.bench.html)
- Will run the closure and print statistics from the benchmarking to stdout. Will persist results under the anonymous label which is shared, making comparisons impossible if running more than one (different) benchmark on the same project, ie. benching two different functions
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_labeled.html)- labeled
- Will run the closure with a label, running with a label enables comparisons for subsequent runs.
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_with_configuration.html)- with_ - configuration
- Will run the benchmark with the supplied configuration
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_with_configuration_labeled.html)- with_ - configuration_ - labeled
- Will run the benchmark with the supplied configuration and a label
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_with_setup.html)- with_ - setup
- Fitting if some setup for the benchmark is required, and that setup should not be timed. The setup will be run prior to each benchmarking run.
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_with_setup_configuration.html)- with_ - setup_ - configuration
- Run bench with setup and configuration
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_with_setup_configuration_labeled.html)- with_ - setup_ - configuration_ - labeled
- Run bench with setup, configuration, and a label
- [bench_](https://docs.rs/fn.bench_with_setup_labeled.html)- with_ - setup_ - labeled
- Run bench with setup and a label
- [black_](https://docs.rs/fn.black_box.html)- box
- An identity function that **hints**`black_box`could do.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_timed.html)- timed
- The simplest possible timed function that just runs some `FnMut`closure and returns the time it took
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_timed_from_iterator.html)- timed_ - from_ - iterator
- Drains an iterator and calls the closure with the yielded value, timing the closure’s execution.
- [run_](https://docs.rs/fn.run_timed_times.html)- timed_ - times
- Runs some closure `n`times and returns the data gathered

# trybuild - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trybuild/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#a-compiler-diagnostics-testing-library-in-just-3-functions) A compiler diagnostics testing library in just 3 functions.

Trybuild is a test harness for invoking rustc on a set of test cases and asserting that any resulting error messages are the ones intended.

Such tests are commonly useful for testing error reporting involving procedural macros. We would write test cases triggering either errors detected by the macro or errors detected by the Rust compiler in the resulting expanded code, and compare against the expected errors to ensure that they remain user-friendly.

This style of testing is sometimes called *ui tests* because they test
aspects of the user’s interaction with a library outside of what would be
covered by ordinary API tests.

Nothing here is specific to macros; trybuild would work equally well for testing misuse of non-macro APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-fail-tests)Compile-fail tests

A minimal trybuild setup looks like this:

```
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild::TestCases::new();
    t.compile_fail("tests/ui/*.rs");
}
```
The test can be run with `cargo test`. It will individually compile each of
the source files matching the glob pattern, expect them to fail to compile,
and assert that the compiler’s error message matches an adjacently named
**.stderr* file containing the expected output (same file name as the test
except with a different extension). If it matches, the test case is
considered to succeed.

Dependencies listed under `[dev-dependencies]` in the project’s Cargo.toml
are accessible from within the test cases.

Failing tests display the expected vs actual compiler output inline.

A compile_fail test that fails to fail to compile is also a failure.

[§](https://docs.rs#pass-tests)Pass tests

The same test harness is able to run tests that are expected to pass, too.
Ordinarily you would just have Cargo run such tests directly, but being able
to combine modes like this could be useful for workshops in which
participants work through test cases enabling one at a time. Trybuild was
originally developed for my [procedural macros workshop at Rust
Latam](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop).

```
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild::TestCases::new();
    t.pass("tests/01-parse-header.rs");
    t.pass("tests/02-parse-body.rs");
    t.compile_fail("tests/03-expand-four-errors.rs");
    t.pass("tests/04-paste-ident.rs");
    t.pass("tests/05-repeat-section.rs");
    //t.pass("tests/06-make-work-in-function.rs");
    //t.pass("tests/07-init-array.rs");
    //t.compile_fail("tests/08-ident-span.rs");
}
```
Pass tests are considered to succeed if they compile successfully and have a
`main` function that does not panic when the compiled binary is executed.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

That’s the entire API.

[§](https://docs.rs#workflow)Workflow

There are two ways to update the **.stderr* files as you iterate on your
test cases or your library; handwriting them is not recommended.

First, if a test case is being run as compile_fail but a corresponding
**.stderr* file does not exist, the test runner will save the actual
compiler output with the right filename into a directory called *wip* within
the directory containing Cargo.toml. So you can update these files by
deleting them, running `cargo test`, and moving all the files from *wip*
into your testcase directory.

Alternatively, run `cargo test` with the environment variable
`TRYBUILD=overwrite` to skip the *wip* directory and write all compiler
output directly in place. You’ll want to check `git diff` afterward to be
sure the compiler’s output is what you had in mind.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-to-test)What to test

When it comes to compile-fail tests, write tests for anything for which you care to find out when there are changes in the user-facing compiler output. As a negative example, please don’t write compile-fail tests simply calling all of your public APIs with arguments of the wrong type; there would be no benefit.

A common use would be for testing specific targeted error messages emitted
by a procedural macro. For example the derive macro from the [ ref-cast](https://github.com/dtolnay/ref-cast)
crate is required to be placed on a type that has either

`#[repr(C)]` or
`#[repr(transparent)]` in order for the expansion to be free of undefined
behavior, which it enforces at compile time:```
error: RefCast trait requires #[repr(C)] or #[repr(transparent)]
 --> $DIR/missing-repr.rs:3:10
  |
3 | #[derive(RefCast)]
  |          ^^^^^^^
```
Macros that consume helper attributes will want to check that unrecognized content within those attributes is properly indicated to the caller. Is the error message correctly placed under the erroneous tokens, not on a useless call_site span?

```
error: unknown serde field attribute `qqq`
 --> $DIR/unknown-attribute.rs:5:13
  |
5 |     #[serde(qqq = "...")]
  |             ^^^
```
Declarative macros can benefit from compile-fail tests too. The [ json!](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/macro.json.html)
macro from serde_json is just a great big macro_rules macro but makes an
effort to have error messages from broken JSON in the input always appear on
the most appropriate token:

```
error: no rules expected the token `,`
 --> $DIR/double-comma.rs:4:38
  |
4 |     println!("{}", json!({ "k": null,, }));
  |                                      ^ no rules expected this token in macro call
```
Sometimes we may have a macro that expands successfully but we count on it
to trigger particular compiler errors at some point beyond macro expansion.
For example the [ readonly](https://github.com/dtolnay/readonly) crate introduces struct fields that are public
but readable only, even if the caller has a &mut reference to the
surrounding struct. If someone writes to a readonly field, we need to be
sure that it wouldn’t compile:

```
error[E0594]: cannot assign to data in a `&` reference
  --> $DIR/write-a-readonly.rs:17:26
   |
17 |     println!("{}", s.n); s.n += 1;
   |                          ^^^^^^^^ cannot assign
```
In all of these cases, the compiler’s output can change because our crate or one of our dependencies broke something, or as a consequence of changes in the Rust compiler. Both are good reasons to have well conceived compile-fail tests. If we refactor and mistakenly cause an error that used to be correct to now no longer be emitted or be emitted in the wrong place, that is important for a test suite to catch. If the compiler changes something that makes error messages that we care about substantially worse, it is also important to catch and report as a compiler issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#troubleshooting)Troubleshooting

The Rust compiler’s diagnostic output can vary as a function of whether the
`rust-src` Rustup component is installed. The compiler will render source
snippets from the standard library if the standard library source is
available locally, and will simply omit snippets if not. This can account
for differences between CI and local development.

If you have compile_fail tests pertaining to standard library traits or types, you can ensure a consistent environment by adding a rust-toolchain.toml file with the following content.

```
[toolchain]
components = ["rust-src"]
```

---

# modular_bitfield - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/modular-bitfield/latest/target-redirect/modular_bitfield/

## Expand description

Provides macros to support bitfield structs allowing for modular use of bit-enums.

The mainly provided macros are [ #[bitfield]](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html) for structs and

[for enums that shall be usable within bitfield structs.](https://docs.rs/trait.Specifier.html)

`#[derive(Specifier)]`There are preset bitfield specifiers such as `B1`, `B2`,..,`B64`
that allow for easy bitfield usage in structs very similar to how
they work in C or C++.

- Performance of the macro generated code is as fast as its hand-written alternative.
- Compile-time checks allow for safe usage of bitfield structs and enums.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Annotate a Rust struct with the [ #[bitfield]](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html) attribute in order to convert it into a bitfield,
with

[optional parameters](https://docs.rs/attr.bitfield.html#parameters)that control how the bitfield is generated. The

`B1`, `B2`, … `B128` prelude types can be used as primitives to declare the number of bits per field.```
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: B1,
    status: B2,
}
```
This produces a `new` constructor as well as a variety of getters and setters that
allows to interact with the bitfield in a safe fashion:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-constructors)Example: Constructors

```
let data = PackedData::new()
    .with_header(1)
    .with_body(2)
    .with_is_alive(0)
    .with_status(3);
assert_eq!(data.header(), 1);
assert_eq!(data.body(), 2);
assert_eq!(data.is_alive(), 0);
assert_eq!(data.status(), 3);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-primitive-types)Example: Primitive Types

Any type that implements the `Specifier` trait can be used as a bitfield field.
Besides the already mentioned `B1`, .. `B128` also the `bool`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`,
`u64` or `u128` primitive types can be used from prelude.

We can use this knowledge to encode our `is_alive` as `bool` type instead of `B1`:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: B2,
}
let mut data = PackedData::new()
    .with_is_alive(true);
assert!(data.is_alive());
data.set_is_alive(false);
assert!(!data.is_alive());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-enum-specifiers)Example: Enum Specifiers

It is possible to derive the `Specifier` trait for `enum` types very easily to make
them also usable as a field within a bitfield type:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow, None,
}
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: Status,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-extra-safety-guard)Example: Extra Safety Guard

In order to make sure that our `Status` enum still requires exatly 2 bit we can add
`#[bits = 2]` to its field:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: B4,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    status: Status,
}
```
Setting and getting our new `status` field is naturally as follows:

```
let mut data = PackedData::new()
    .with_status(Status::Green);
assert_eq!(data.status(), Status::Green);
data.set_status(Status::Red);
assert_eq!(data.status(), Status::Red);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-skipping-fields)Example: Skipping Fields

It might make sense to only allow users to set or get information from a field or
even to entirely disallow interaction with a bitfield. For this the `#[skip]` attribute
can be used on a bitfield of a `#[bitfield]` annotated struct.

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct SomeBitsUndefined {
    #[skip(setters)]
    read_only: bool,
    #[skip(getters)]
    write_only: bool,
    #[skip]
    unused: B6,
}
```
It is possible to use `#[skip(getters, setters)]` or `#[skip(getters)]` followed by a `#[skip(setters)]`
attribute applied on the same bitfield. The effects are the same. When skipping both, getters and setters,
it is possible to completely avoid having to specify a name:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct SomeBitsUndefined {
    #[skip] __: B2,
    is_activ: bool,
    #[skip] __: B2,
    is_received: bool,
    #[skip] __: B2,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-unfilled-bitfields)Example: Unfilled Bitfields

Sometimes it might be useful to not be required to construct a bitfield that defines
all bits and therefore is required to have a bit width divisible by 8. In this case
you can use the `filled: bool` parameter of the `#[bitfield]` macro in order to toggle
this for your respective bitfield:

```
#[bitfield(filled = false)]
pub struct SomeBitsUndefined {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    pre_status: B3,
}
```
In the above example `SomeBitsUndefined` only defines the first 5 bits and leaves the rest
3 bits of its entire 8 bits undefined. The consequences are that its generated `from_bytes`
method is fallible since it must guard against those undefined bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-recursive-bitfields)Example: Recursive Bitfields

It is possible to use `#[bitfield]` structs as fields of `#[bitfield]` structs.
This is generally useful if there are some common fields for multiple bitfields
and is achieved by adding the `#[derive(Specifier)]` attribute to the struct
annotated with `#[bitfield]`:

```
#[bitfield(filled = false)]
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub struct Header {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    pre_status: Status,
}
#[bitfield]
pub struct PackedData {
    header: Header,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    status: Status,
}
```
With the `bits: int` parameter of the `#[bitfield]` macro on the `Header` struct and the
`#[bits: int]` attribute of the `#[derive(Specifier)]` on the `Status` enum we
can have additional compile-time guarantees about the bit widths of the resulting entities:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
#[bits = 2]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow, None,
}
#[bitfield(bits = 4)]
#[derive(Specifier)]
pub struct Header {
    is_compact: bool,
    is_secure: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    pre_status: Status,
}
#[bitfield(bits = 16)]
pub struct PackedData {
    #[bits = 4]
    header: Header,
    body: B9,
    is_alive: bool,
    #[bits = 2]
    status: Status,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-advanced-enum-specifiers)Example: Advanced Enum Specifiers

For our `Status` enum we actually just need 3 status variants: `Green`, `Yellow` and `Red`.
We introduced the `None` status variants because `Specifier` enums by default are required
to have a number of variants that is a power of two. We can ship around this by specifying
`#[bits = 2]` on the top and get rid of our placeholder `None` variant while maintaining
the invariant of it requiring 2 bits:

```
#[derive(Specifier)]
#[bits = 2]
pub enum Status {
    Red, Green, Yellow,
}
```
However, having such enums now yields the possibility that a bitfield might contain invalid bit
patterns for such fields. We can safely access those fields with protected getters. For the sake
of demonstration we will use the generated `from_bytes` constructor with which we can easily
construct bitfields that may contain invalid bit patterns:

```
let mut data = PackedData::from_bytes([0b0000_0000, 0b1100_0000]);
//           The 2 status field bits are invalid -----^^
//           as Red = 0x00, Green = 0x01 and Yellow = 0x10
assert_eq!(data.status_or_err(), Err(InvalidBitPattern::new(0b11)));
data.set_status(Status::Green);
assert_eq!(data.status_or_err(), Ok(Status::Green));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#generated-implementations)Generated Implementations

For the example `#[bitfield]` struct the following implementations are going to be generated:

```
#[bitfield]
pub struct Example {
    a: bool,
    b: B7,
}
```
| Signature | Description |
|---|---|
| `fn new() -> Self` | Creates a new instance of the bitfield with all bits initialized to 0. |
| `fn from_bytes([u8; 1]) -> Self` | Creates a new instance of the bitfield from the given raw bytes. |
| `fn into_bytes(self) -> [u8; 1]` | Returns the underlying bytes of the bitfield. |

And below the generated signatures for field `a`:

| Signature | Description |
|---|---|
| `fn a() -> bool` | Returns the value of `a`or panics if invalid. |
| `fn a_or_err() -> Result<bool, InvalidBitPattern<u8>>` | Returns the value of `a`of an error providing information about the invalid bits. |
| `fn set_a(&mut self, new_value: bool)` | Sets `a`to the new value or panics if`new_value`contains invalid bits. |
| `fn set_a_checked(&mut self, new_value: bool) -> Result<(), OutOfBounds>` | Sets `a`to the new value of returns an out of bounds error. |
| `fn with_a(self, new_value: bool) -> Self` | Similar to `set_a`but useful for method chaining. |
| `fn with_a_checked(self, new_value: bool) -> Result<Self, OutOfBounds>` | Similar to `set_a_checked`but useful for method chaining. |

Getters for unnamed fields in tuple-like structs are prefixed with `get_`
(e.g. `get_0()`, `get_1_or_err()`, etc.).

[§](https://docs.rs#generated-structure)Generated Structure

From David Tolnay’s procedural macro workshop:

The macro conceptualizes given structs as a sequence of bits 0..N. The bits are grouped into fields in the order specified by the struct written by the user.

The `#[bitfield]` attribute rewrites the caller’s struct into a private byte array representation
with public getter and setter methods for each field.
The total number of bits N is required to be a multiple of 8: This is checked at compile time.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following invocation builds a struct with a total size of 32 bits or 4 bytes.
It places field `a` in the least significant bit of the first byte,
field `b` in the next three least significant bits,
field `c` in the remaining four most significant bits of the first byte,
and field `d` spanning the next three bytes.

```
use modular_bitfield::prelude::*;
#[bitfield]
pub struct MyFourBytes {
    a: B1,
    b: B3,
    c: B4,
    d: B24,
}
```
```
                               least significant bit of third byte
                                 ┊           most significant
                                 ┊             ┊
                                 ┊             ┊
║  first byte   ║  second byte  ║  third byte   ║  fourth byte  ║
╟───────────────╫───────────────╫───────────────╫───────────────╢
║▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒ ▒║
╟─╫─────╫───────╫───────────────────────────────────────────────╢
║a║  b  ║   c   ║                       d                       ║
                 ┊                                             ┊
                 ┊                                             ┊
               least significant bit of d         most significant
```

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# cognee-lib

Unified public API for cognee-rust — the single-entry-point umbrella crate that re-exports `add`, `cognify`, and `search` for embedded and Rust-SDK users.

Part of [cognee-rs](https://github.com/topoteretes/cognee-rs) — see the [project README](https://docs.rs/README.md) for an architecture overview and how the pieces fit together.

# snowbridge_pallet_inbound_queue_v2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snowbridge-pallet-inbound-queue-v2/0.14.0/snowbridge_pallet_inbound_queue_v2/

## Expand description

Inbound Queue

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

Receives messages emitted by the Gateway contract on Ethereum, whereupon they are verified, translated to XCM, and finally sent to AssetHub for further processing.

Message relayers are rewarded in wrapped Ether that is included within the message. This wrapped Ether is derived from Ether that the message origin has locked up on Ethereum.

[§](https://docs.rs#extrinsics)Extrinsics

[§](https://docs.rs#governance)Governance

- `Call::set_operating_mode`

[§](https://docs.rs#message-submission)Message Submission

- `Call::submit`

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::weights::`- [WeightInfo](https://docs.rs/weights/trait.WeightInfo.html);
- `pub use`- [pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [pallet](https://docs.rs/pallet/index.html)
- The `pallet`module in each FRAME pallet hosts the most important items needed to construct this pallet.
- [weights](https://docs.rs/weights/index.html)
- Autogenerated weights for `snowbridge_inbound_queue`

# aegis-id 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/aegis-id/0.1.0

# Aegis ID

Aegis ID is a terminal password-rule puzzle disguised as a very ordinary account enrollment console.

The program asks for a username and password, then quietly adds increasingly restrictive password requirements. Failed attempts only show the requirements that are currently not satisfied. Once every rule is satisfied, the console clears and asks you to rewrite the password exactly.

## Install

```
```
## Run

```
```
Press `Ctrl-C` to quit.

# graphtrail - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/graphtrail/0.2.0/graphtrail/

## Expand description

GraphTrail: a local code-graph sidecar. Library crate exposing the extraction, storage, and query layers so the CLI binary, tests, and (later) the MCP server share one API.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [adapters](https://docs.rs/adapters/index.html)
- Optional, feature-gated integrations with external systems. The default build compiles none of these, keeping the core sidecar free of network and cross-tool dependencies.
- [cli](https://docs.rs/cli/index.html)
- Command-line surface and output formatting.
- [extractors](https://docs.rs/extractors/index.html)
- File indexing: language detection and per-file extraction dispatch.
- [mcp](https://docs.rs/mcp/index.html)
- Minimal MCP server: newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdin/stdout, exposing GraphTrail’s read-only queries as tools. No async runtime and no extra dependencies, keeping the sidecar small.
- [model](https://docs.rs/model/index.html)
- Shared plain-data types used across extractors, store, and query layers.
- [query](https://docs.rs/query/index.html)
- Read-only query layer over the graph database.
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- Storage layer: schema, connection lifecycle, and the sync write path.

---

# oxvif - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/oxvif/0.11.0/oxvif/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#oxvif)oxvif

An async Rust client library for the [ONVIF](https://www.onvif.org) IP camera protocol.

ONVIF (Open Network Video Interface Forum) is the industry standard for interoperability between IP-based security cameras. This library provides a complete async client covering device management, media streaming, PTZ control, imaging, on-screen display, events, recording, search, and replay — all over SOAP/HTTP(S) with WS-Security and HTTP Digest authentication.

[§](https://docs.rs#onvif-profile-coverage)ONVIF Profile coverage

| Profile | Description | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Profile S | Video streaming | ~95% | All core operations implemented |
| Profile T | Advanced streaming (H.265, focus, OSD, audio) | ~95% | HTTP Digest Auth, Media2 audio/metadata/analytics config, PTZ compat; Analytics rules and DeviceIO not yet implemented |
| Profile G | Recording & playback | ~85% | Read/search/replay + full recording/job write management; live-source job binding not yet implemented |

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-services)Supported services

- **Device**— capabilities, scopes, device info, hostname, NTP, reboot, user management, network interfaces/protocols/DNS/gateway, relay outputs, storage configurations, system log/URIs, factory default, discovery mode, firmware upgrade / system restore (upload-URI flow), auxiliary commands (wiper/IR lamp)
- **Media1 / Media2**— profiles, RTSP/snapshot URIs, video + audio config, OSD, metadata config, audio decoder/output config, video source modes, unified AddConfiguration/RemoveConfiguration
- **PTZ**— absolute/relative/continuous move, presets, home position, status, configurations, nodes, compatible configurations
- **Imaging**— brightness/contrast/exposure settings, focus move/stop/status
- **Events**— pull-point subscriptions, event polling, renew, unsubscribe, continuous- `event_stream`, synchronization point
- **Recording**— list stored recordings; create/delete recordings, tracks, and recording jobs
- **Search**— find recordings by scope, collect results, end search
- **Replay**— get RTSP playback URI for a stored recording
- **WS-Discovery**— UDP multicast probe to find cameras on the local network

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

- `health`- `health::HealthCheck`, a fast read-only conformance check that returns a- `health::HealthReport`(per-check Pass/Warn/Fail/Skip plus a Profile S/T/G assessment). Pure library code over- `OnvifSession`- `to_json`/- `to_json_pretty`) and a later report can diff against an earlier one via- `HealthReport::diff`- `examples/healthcheck.rs --baseline <file.json>`.
- `mock`- `mock-server`- `mock`module). The- `mock`feature also exposes- `fixtures::CapturingTransport`/- `fixtures::FixtureTransport`for recording real-camera exchanges into- `tests/fixtures/<vendor>-<model>/`and replaying them in tests without the device (see- `examples/record_fixtures.rs`).

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  OnvifSession                        │
│     caches service URLs — delegates every call       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                   OnvifClient                        │
│     stateless — you supply service URLs per call     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│    soap::SoapEnvelope  │  soap::WsSecurityToken      │  ← SOAP layer
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                  Transport trait                     │  ← HTTP abstraction
│          (HttpTransport / mock in tests)             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

Two ways to use oxvif — pick whichever suits your workflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#onvifsession--url-caching-handled-for-you)`OnvifSession` — URL caching handled for you

[ OnvifSession](https://docs.rs/session/struct.OnvifSession.html) calls

`GetCapabilities` once at construction and caches all
service URLs. No URL parameters needed for individual methods.```
use oxvif::{OnvifSession, OnvifError};
async fn run() -> Result<(), OnvifError> {
    let session = OnvifSession::builder("http://192.168.1.100/onvif/device_service")
        .with_credentials("admin", "password")
        .with_clock_sync()  // syncs WS-Security timestamp with device clock
        .build()
        .await?;
    let profiles = session.get_profiles().await?;
    let uri = session.get_stream_uri(&profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("RTSP stream: {}", uri.uri);
    let status = session.ptz_get_status(&profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("Pan: {:?}  Tilt: {:?}", status.pan, status.tilt);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#onvifclient--direct-control-you-manage-service-urls)`OnvifClient` — direct control, you manage service URLs

[ OnvifClient](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OnvifClient.html) is stateless and gives direct control over every call.
You fetch and forward service URLs yourself for full routing control.

```
use oxvif::{OnvifClient, OnvifError};
async fn run() -> Result<(), OnvifError> {
    let client = OnvifClient::new("http://192.168.1.100/onvif/device_service")
        .with_credentials("admin", "password");
    let dt = client.get_system_date_and_time().await?;
    let client = client.with_utc_offset(dt.utc_offset_secs());
    let caps = client.get_capabilities().await?;
    let media_url = caps.media.url.as_deref().unwrap();
    let profiles = client.get_profiles(media_url).await?;
    let uri = client.get_stream_uri(media_url, &profiles[0].token).await?;
    println!("RTSP stream: {}", uri.uri);
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing-without-a-real-camera)Testing without a real camera

Enable the ** mock** feature for a built-in, stateful mock ONVIF device and
drive an

[against it — no network, no real camera. The](https://docs.rs/client/struct.OnvifClient.html)

`OnvifClient`**feature additionally provides a bound-port**

`mock-server``mock::MockServer`
for cross-process / non-Rust clients. See the `mock` module for details.[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Cargo.toml:  oxvif = { version = "0.9", features = ["mock"] }
use std::sync::Arc;
use oxvif::{OnvifClient, mock::MockTransport};
let client = OnvifClient::new("http://mock")
    .with_transport(Arc::new(MockTransport::new()));
// exercise client commands — Set persists, Get reflects it.
```
For full control you can instead implement [ transport::Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) yourself
to inject any fixture:

```
use oxvif::transport::{Transport, TransportError};
use async_trait::async_trait;
use std::sync::Arc;
struct FixtureTransport { xml: String }
#[async_trait]
impl Transport for FixtureTransport {
    async fn soap_post(&self, _url: &str, _action: &str, _body: String)
        -> Result<String, TransportError>
    {
        Ok(self.xml.clone())
    }
}
let client = oxvif::OnvifClient::new("http://ignored")
    .with_transport(Arc::new(FixtureTransport { xml: "<s:Envelope/>".into() }));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#health--conformance-checks)Health & conformance checks

Enable the ** health** feature for

[— a fast, read-only conformance check that reports Pass/Warn/Fail/Skip per ONVIF service plus a Profile S/T/G verdict. It includes a](https://docs.rs/health/struct.HealthCheck.html)

`health::HealthCheck`**parse-coverage**dimension that flags when a parser silently drops list data (a wrong element name returning an empty result with no error). To validate the parsers against real hardware, the

`conformance` example dumps each device’s raw
responses next to the parsed summary so silent-parse gaps stand out.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- High-level ONVIF client.
- [discovery](https://docs.rs/discovery/index.html)
- WS-Discovery — UDP multicast device probe.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Top-level error type for the oxvif library.
- [fixtures](https://docs.rs/fixtures/index.html)
- Record-and-replay SOAP transports for fixture-based testing.
- [health](https://docs.rs/health/index.html)
- Fast, scriptable ONVIF health / conformance check for a target device.
- [mock](https://docs.rs/mock/index.html)
- In-process / bound-port mock ONVIF device for testing client code without a real camera.
- [session](https://docs.rs/session/index.html)
- High-level session wrapper around `OnvifClient`
- [soap](https://docs.rs/soap/index.html)
- SOAP protocol layer for ONVIF.
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- HTTP transport abstraction for SOAP over HTTP/HTTPS.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)
- Typed response structs for all ONVIF operations.

# rsclaw-migrate 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-migrate/0.1.0

Please check the

[build logs](https://docs.rs/crate/rsclaw-migrate/0.1.0/builds)for more information.

See

[Builds](https://docs.rs/about/builds)for ideas on how to fix a failed build, or

[Metadata](https://docs.rs/about/metadata)for how to configure docs.rs builds.

If you believe this is docs.rs' fault,

[open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose).

OpenClaw data migration module.

Provides three migration modes for transitioning from OpenClaw to rsclaw:

- `Seamless`: coexist with OpenClaw, sharing base directory
- `Import`: copy all OpenClaw data into rsclaw's own stores
- `New`: ignore OpenClaw data entirely, start new

OpenClaw stores data as JSONL files, not SQLite. The directory layout is: ~/.openclaw/ openclaw.json # Main config agents/<agent_id>/sessions/sessions.json # Session index agents/<agent_id>/sessions/.jsonl # Session messages agents/<agent_id>/agent/auth-profiles.json # API keys

---

# polkadot_node_subsystem_util - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-node-subsystem-util/32.0.0/polkadot_node_subsystem_util/

## Expand description

Utility module for subsystems

Many subsystems have common interests such as canceling a bunch of spawned jobs, or determining what their validator ID is. These common interests are factored into this module.

This crate also reexports Prometheus metric types which are expected to be implemented by subsystems.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [availability_](https://docs.rs/availability_chunks/index.html)- chunks
- Helpers for the validator->chunk index mapping.
- [backing_](https://docs.rs/backing_implicit_view/index.html)- implicit_ - view
- A utility for managing the implicit view of the relay-chain derived from active leaves and the minimum allowed relay-parents that parachain candidates can have and be backed in those leaves’ children.
- [database](https://docs.rs/database/index.html)
- Database trait for subsystem. Database trait for polkadot db.
- [inclusion_](https://docs.rs/inclusion_emulator/index.html)- emulator
- An emulator for node-side code to predict the results of on-chain parachain inclusion and predict future constraints.
- [metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/index.html)
- This module reexports Prometheus types and defines the `Metrics`
- [nesting_](https://docs.rs/nesting_sender/index.html)- sender
- Nested message sending
- [reexports](https://docs.rs/reexports/index.html)
- These reexports are required so that external crates can use the `delegated_subsystem`macro properly.
- [reputation](https://docs.rs/reputation/index.html)
- A utility abstraction to collect and send reputation changes.
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Convenient and efficient runtime info access. Convenient interface to runtime information.
- [vstaging](https://docs.rs/vstaging/index.html)
- Helpers for working with unreleased runtime calls Contains helpers for staging runtime calls.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Controlled](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlledValidatorIndices.html)- Validator - Indices
- Keeps track of the validator indices controlled by the local validator in a given session. For better performance, the values for each session are cached.
- [Metronome](https://docs.rs/struct.Metronome.html)
- Create a stream of ticks with a defined cycle duration.
- [Timeout](https://docs.rs/struct.Timeout.html)
- A future that wraps another future with a `Delay`allowing for time-limited futures.
- [Validator](https://docs.rs/struct.Validator.html)
- Local validator information

- Result of `check_relay_parent_session`
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Utility errors
- [Overseer](https://docs.rs/enum.OverseerError.html)- Error

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [JOB_](https://docs.rs/constant.JOB_CHANNEL_CAPACITY.html)- CHANNEL_ - CAPACITY
- Capacity of channels to and from individual jobs
- [JOB_](https://docs.rs/constant.JOB_GRACEFUL_STOP_DURATION.html)- GRACEFUL_ - STOP_ - DURATION
- Duration a job will wait after sending a stop signal before hard-aborting.
- [MIN_](https://docs.rs/constant.MIN_GOSSIP_PEERS.html)- GOSSIP_ - PEERS
- The minimum amount of peers to send gossip messages to.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_relay_parent_session.html)- relay_ - parent_ - session
- Check whether a relay parent is valid in a given session.
- [choose_](https://docs.rs/fn.choose_random_subset.html)- random_ - subset
- Choose a random subset of `min`elements. But always include`is_priority`elements.
- [choose_](https://docs.rs/fn.choose_random_subset_with_rng.html)- random_ - subset_ - with_ - rng
- Choose a random subset of `min`elements using a specific Random Generator`Rng`But always include`is_priority`elements.
- [determine_](https://docs.rs/fn.determine_new_blocks.html)- new_ - blocks
- Given a new chain-head hash, this determines the hashes of all new blocks we should track metadata for, given this head.
- [executor_](https://docs.rs/fn.executor_params_at_relay_parent.html)- params_ - at_ - relay_ - parent
- Requests executor parameters from the runtime effective at given relay-parent. First obtains
session index at the relay-parent, relying on the fact that it should be cached by the runtime
API caching layer even if the block itself has already been pruned. Then requests executor
parameters by session index.
Returns an error if failed to communicate to the runtime, or the parameters are not in the
storage, which should never happen.
Returns default execution parameters if the runtime doesn’t yet support `SessionExecutorParams`API call. Otherwise, returns execution parameters returned by the runtime.
- [fetch_](https://docs.rs/fn.fetch_relay_parent_info.html)- relay_ - parent_ - info
- Fetch relay parent info for a block, including the block being queried at.
- [find_](https://docs.rs/fn.find_validator_group.html)- validator_ - group
- Find the validator group the given validator index belongs to.
- [gen_](https://docs.rs/fn.gen_ratio.html)- ratio
- Returns a `bool`with a probability of`a / b`of being true.
- [gen_](https://docs.rs/fn.gen_ratio_rng.html)- ratio_ - rng
- Returns a `bool`with a probability of`a / b`of being true.
- [has_](https://docs.rs/fn.has_required_runtime.html)- required_ - runtime
- Verifies if `ParachainHost`runtime api is at least at version`required_runtime_version`. This method is used to determine if a given runtime call is supported by the runtime.

# autoconf_rs_cli - Rust

autoconf-rs-cli shared library.

Provides the CLI argument parsing harness used by all 8 Autoconf binaries. Each binary is a thin wrapper that delegates to autoconf-rs-core.
